qs.q: An infant presents with cyanosis and a chest radiograph revealing a classic boot-shaped heart. Echocardiography confirms a combination of right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, and a septal defect. What is the primary congenital diagnosis?
qs.e: Tetralogy of Fallot includes a ventricular septal defect, right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta, and pulmonary stenosis, producing a boot-shaped heart on chest radiography. Transposition of the great arteries classically presents with an egg-on-string CXR.

ai.title: Pulmonary Stenosis in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Pulmonary stenosis is a narrowing of the pulmonary valve or outflow tract, obstructing blood flow from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery. It is a common congenital heart defect, often presenting with a characteristic murmur. Severity dictates clinical presentation and management.

sections.p: Pulmonary stenosis is an obstruction to blood flow from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery. This obstruction can occur at the valve (valvular PS), below the valve (subvalvular PS), or above the valve (supravalvular PS). Valvular PS is the most common type. The diagnosis is primarily made by clinical examination and confirmed by echocardiography.
b: Valvular PS: Most common, narrowing at the pulmonary valve leaflets.
Subvalvular PS: Obstruction below the valve, often due to muscular hypertrophy.
Supravalvular PS: Narrowing above the valve, in the main pulmonary artery or its branches.

sections.p: The severity of pulmonary stenosis is determined by the pressure gradient across the obstruction and the degree of right ventricular hypertrophy. This classification guides management decisions.
b: Mild PS: Peak gradient less than 30 mmHg. Usually asymptomatic, good prognosis.
Moderate PS: Peak gradient 30-50 mmHg. May have mild symptoms, requires monitoring.
Severe PS: Peak gradient greater than 50 mmHg. Often symptomatic, increased risk of complications, requires intervention.
Critical PS: Presents in neonates with severe cyanosis and duct-dependent pulmonary circulation.

sections.p: Pulmonary stenosis is predominantly a congenital heart defect, often isolated but can be part of more complex syndromes. Acquired causes are rare in children.
b: Congenital: Most common cause, often isolated malformation of the pulmonary valve leaflets (dysplastic, bicuspid, or fused).
Associated with syndromes: Noonan syndrome, Alagille syndrome, Tetralogy of Fallot (PS is one of the four features: VSD, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy).
Rheumatic heart disease: Very rare cause of acquired pulmonary stenosis, typically affecting the mitral and aortic valves more commonly.

sections.p: The presentation of pulmonary stenosis varies significantly with its severity. Mild cases may be asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, while severe cases can present with significant symptoms.
b: Asymptomatic: Often in mild to moderate cases, discovered during routine examination.
Fatigue and dyspnoea on exertion: Due to reduced cardiac output and right ventricular strain.
Cyanosis: In severe or critical PS, especially in neonates, due to right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale or VSD.
Syncope or chest pain: Rare, but can occur with severe right ventricular outflow obstruction.
Ejection systolic murmur: Heard best at the left upper sternal border, often harsh and loud.
Thrill: Palpable at the left upper sternal border in moderate to severe cases.
Right ventricular heave: Palpable in severe PS due to right ventricular hypertrophy.
Prominent 'a' waves in jugular venous pulse: Indicative of increased right atrial pressure due to right ventricular outflow obstruction.
Wide splitting of the second heart sound: Due to delayed pulmonary valve closure from prolonged right ventricular ejection.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm the diagnosis, assess severity, and identify associated anomalies. Availability of advanced imaging may vary in low-resource settings, making clinical examination and basic tests crucial.

t.b: Does the child have a heart murmur or signs of right heart strain? A loud, harsh ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border with a palpable thrill and wide splitting of S2 suggests pulmonary stenosis. An inaudible pulmonary closure sound (P2) suggests severe PS.

Is there evidence of right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) or right atrial enlargement? RVH suggests significant right ventricular pressure overload. In low-resource settings, this is a readily available and important screening tool.

Are there signs of cardiomegaly, pulmonary artery dilatation, or decreased pulmonary vascular markings? Post-stenotic dilatation of the main pulmonary artery is common. Decreased pulmonary vascularity suggests severe obstruction. This is often available when echocardiography is not.

What is the anatomy of the pulmonary valve and outflow tract, and what is the pressure gradient? This is the definitive diagnostic test, providing detailed anatomical and functional assessment, including severity grading. If unavailable, clinical assessment, ECG, and CXR guide initial management and referral.

What is the precise pressure gradient across the pulmonary valve and can it be treated interventionally? Used for accurate pressure measurement and often for balloon valvuloplasty in severe cases. This is an invasive procedure and less commonly available in low-resource settings.

sections.p: Recognising red flags is crucial for timely intervention and preventing severe complications, especially in children with moderate to severe pulmonary stenosis.
b: Progressive cyanosis: Especially in neonates, indicating critical PS and duct-dependent circulation.
Signs of right heart failure: Hepatomegaly, peripheral oedema, ascites, suggesting severe right ventricular strain.
Syncope or chest pain: Warning signs of severe outflow obstruction and myocardial ischaemia.
Sudden deterioration: May indicate acute right heart failure or arrhythmias.
Paradoxical embolism: Risk in cyanotic patients with a patent foramen ovale, especially with dehydration.
Infective endocarditis: Risk in unrepaired cyanotic heart disease, requiring prophylaxis in certain situations.

sections.p: Management depends on the severity of the stenosis. The goal is to relieve the obstruction and prevent complications. In low-resource settings, conservative management and timely referral for intervention are key.
b: Mild PS: Regular follow-up, no intervention usually needed. Monitor for progression.
Moderate PS: Regular follow-up, consider intervention if symptomatic or if RVH progresses.
Severe PS: Intervention is usually required. Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty is the preferred first-line treatment.
Critical PS (neonates): Prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency, followed by urgent balloon valvuloplasty or surgical repair.
Surgical valvotomy or patch augmentation: Considered if balloon valvuloplasty is unsuccessful or anatomically unsuitable.
Prophylaxis for infective endocarditis: Recommended for unrepaired cyanotic heart disease and for the first 6 months after repair with prosthetic material or if residual defects remain.

sections.p: Lifelong follow-up is essential for all patients with pulmonary stenosis, even after successful intervention, to monitor for residual stenosis, regurgitation, or right ventricular dysfunction.
b: Regular cardiology reviews: To assess for residual or recurrent stenosis/regurgitation and right ventricular function.
Activity restrictions: May be necessary for severe unrepaired PS, but most patients can lead normal lives after successful intervention.
Genetic counselling: Offered if part of a known genetic syndrome.
Prevention of infective endocarditis: Adherence to prophylaxis guidelines for at-risk individuals.

sections.p: Several other conditions can present with heart murmurs or similar symptoms, requiring careful differentiation from pulmonary stenosis.
b: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD): Can have a harsh systolic murmur, but typically loudest at the left lower sternal border and often associated with signs of left-to-right shunt and heart failure.
Aortic Stenosis: Ejection systolic murmur, but loudest at the right upper sternal border and radiates to the neck.
Physiological murmur (Still's murmur): Common in children, typically soft, vibratory, and changes with position, without other signs of heart disease.
Pulmonary Regurgitation: Diastolic murmur, not systolic, heard at the left upper sternal border.

sections.p: Interpreting results requires clinical context, as some findings can be misleading or require careful consideration.
b: Normal ECG: Does not rule out mild pulmonary stenosis, as significant RVH may not be present.
Absent murmur: In critical PS, severe right ventricular failure can lead to reduced flow and a soft or absent murmur.
Normal CXR: Mild PS may have a normal CXR, and the degree of pulmonary artery dilatation does not always correlate with severity.
Echocardiography in uncooperative child: Poor acoustic windows can lead to inaccurate gradient measurements, requiring sedation or repeat studies.

whenToSeekHelp: Increasing cyanosis or blueness of lips/fingers
Poor feeding or failure to thrive in infants
Swelling of the abdomen or legs

faq.q: Can pulmonary stenosis resolve on its own?
faq.a: Mild pulmonary stenosis can sometimes improve or remain stable, but moderate to severe cases usually require intervention and do not resolve spontaneously.
While often sporadic, pulmonary stenosis can be associated with genetic syndromes (e.g., Noonan syndrome), and there can be a slightly increased risk in first-degree relatives.

faq.q: What activities should a child with pulmonary stenosis avoid?
faq.a: Children with mild or successfully repaired PS usually have no restrictions. Those with severe unrepaired PS may need to avoid strenuous physical activity, as advised by their cardiologist.

exam: A 3-month-old presents with increasing cyanosis and poor feeding. On examination, you note a loud ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border and a single S2. What is your immediate management plan, especially considering a low-resource setting? — Stabilise with oxygen and IV fluids, consider prostaglandin E1 if critical PS is suspected to maintain ductal patency, arrange urgent echocardiography if available, and prepare for immediate referral for intervention.

You are on a rural paediatric ward and suspect moderate pulmonary stenosis in a 5-year-old. Echocardiography is not available. What investigations would you perform, and what findings would support your diagnosis? — ECG for RVH and right atrial enlargement; Chest X-ray for cardiomegaly and post-stenotic pulmonary artery dilatation or decreased pulmonary vascularity. Clinical signs like a loud, harsh ejection systolic murmur, thrill, and wide S2 splitting are crucial.

A child with known severe pulmonary stenosis is scheduled for dental extraction. What prophylactic measures, if any, are needed? — Prophylaxis for infective endocarditis is recommended for unrepaired cyanotic heart disease and for the first 6 months after repair with prosthetic material or if residual defects remain. Assess the child's specific repair status.

Describe the key auscultatory findings in severe pulmonary stenosis and explain their physiological basis. — Loud, harsh ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border (turbulent flow across the narrowed valve); wide splitting of the second heart sound (delayed pulmonary valve closure due to prolonged RV ejection); often an inaudible P2 (reduced pulmonary blood flow and valve mobility).

A neonate with critical pulmonary stenosis is started on prostaglandin E1. Explain the mechanism of action and the potential side effects you would monitor for. — Prostaglandin E1 maintains patency of the ductus arteriosus, allowing blood flow to the pulmonary arteries. Monitor for apnoea, fever, flushing, hypotension, and bradycardia.

How would you differentiate the murmur of pulmonary stenosis from that of a ventricular septal defect (VSD) in a child? — PS murmur is ejection systolic, loudest at the left upper sternal border, often with wide S2 splitting. VSD murmur is typically holosystolic, loudest at the left lower sternal border, and often associated with signs of left-to-right shunt and heart failure.

What are the four anatomical features of Tetralogy of Fallot, and how does pulmonary stenosis contribute to its pathophysiology? — The four features are VSD, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Pulmonary stenosis is the key determinant of severity, dictating the degree of right ventricular outflow obstruction and thus the amount of right-to-left shunting and cyanosis.
